lead.topic: Conservation evolution and amphibian host-pathogen immunity
lead.headline: Immunization can help frogs survive chytrid
lead.deck: A synthesis of 36 studies finds that some experimental immunization approaches reduce fungal infections or deaths in amphibians.
lead.authors: Chung MHJ, Duncan RP, Noble DWA, Scheele BC, Clulow S
paragraphs: The chytrid fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis has contributed to amphibian declines around the world, but protecting wild frogs from it remains difficult. Meng-Han Joseph Chung and colleagues asked whether experimental immunization can reduce the damage. They pooled 208 effect sizes from 36 studies involving 22 amphibian species. The studies compared animals that received some form of prior immunization with untreated animals after exposure to the fungus. Rather than treating protection as one outcome, the team separately assessed how often animals became infected, how heavily infected they were, and whether they died.

Immunization using live pathogens was associated with lower fungal loads and reduced mortality after re-exposure. Treatments using natural chemicals derived from the fungus reduced infection prevalence, the proportion of animals testing positive. Other immunization approaches did not produce statistically clear benefits across the assembled studies. Responses also differed with life stage, host group and timing during infection. This is important evidence that acquired protection is possible, not proof that a single vaccine works for every threatened frog. The authors suggest immunization could aid reintroductions, but outcomes in complex wild populations still need direct testing.
lead.push: The immediate test is persistence. If frogs are immunized before release, does protection survive metamorphosis, seasonal change and repeated exposure in natural ponds? A randomized release study could compare survival and infection in immunized and control cohorts while monitoring whether any benefit persists into the next generation, when offspring may be unprotected.

people.name: Meng-Han Joseph Chung
people.bio: Meng-Han Joseph Chung is a postdoctoral research fellow in ecology and genomics at the University of Canberra. He earned his PhD at the Australian National University in 2023, studying fish life histories and sexual selection. His current work examines whether immunization can help threatened frogs resist chytrid disease, including across metamorphosis.

people.name: Simon Clulow
people.bio: Simon Clulow is an associate professor in conservation ecology at the University of Canberra. He studies threatened amphibians and reptiles, invasive species, and wildlife disease. His team develops practical conservation interventions, including warm refuges that limit chytrid fungus and experimental immunization of frogs being returned to habitats where the disease persists.

slot2.headline: Evolution follows the genetic links between traits
slot2.body: Natural selection rarely acts on a single trait in isolation. In a 1979 paper, Russell Lande developed a quantitative genetic account of how correlated characters evolve together. The key insight is that response depends not just on selection for each trait but on the genetic variances and covariances connecting them. He applied the framework to brain and body size, using evidence from mouse selection experiments and mammalian comparisons to examine their joint evolutionary trajectories. The work helped establish multivariate quantitative genetics as a language for studying evolutionary constraint, correlated responses and the directions in which populations can most readily change.

slot3.headline: An elevator sends a message using gravity
slot3.body: A physicist's unlikely transmitter was a university elevator. At the University of Queensland, researchers moved its 1.8-tonne counterweight between two positions to encode binary digits. A sensitive gravimeter on the other side of a brick wall detected the tiny changes in gravitational pull. The team reconstructed the word 'Gravity' across roughly 0.7 metres, transmitting one bit per minute. The experiment, published online on 18 November, demonstrates that ordinary walls cannot screen gravitational signals as they can some electromagnetic ones. It is far from a usable communication system: longer ranges and faster messages depend on proposed sensor improvements, not demonstrated performance.
